823	    /// Convert to pretty-printed document.
824	    ///
825	    /// For example, a binary tree of depth two may print as `(1 (2 3 4) (5 6 7))`,
826	    /// showing each thread ID grouped with its children.
827	    ///
828	    /// The thread_group_leaders argument is used for additional context into account when
829	    /// pretty-printing a `ThreadTree`.  This will indicate which children are within new
830	    /// thread groups using square brackets:
831	    ///
832	    ///   `[1 [2 [3] 4] (5 6 7)]`
833	    // TODO: it would also be nice to store a fixed prefix of the binary name and listing
834	    // that along with the thread ID.
835	    pub fn pretty_print(&self) -> String {
836	        fn walk<'a>(
837	            tt: &'a HashMap<DetTid, Vec<DetTid>>,
838	            tgl: &HashSet<DetTid>,
839	            current: &DetTid,
840	        ) -> RcDoc<'a, ()> {
841	            if let Some(children) = tt.get(current) {
842	                if tgl.contains(current) {
843	                    RcDoc::text("[")
844	                        .append(RcDoc::as_string(current))
845	                        .append(if children.is_empty() {
846	                            RcDoc::text("")
847	                        } else {
848	                            RcDoc::text(" ").append(
849	                                RcDoc::intersperse(
850	                                    children.iter().map(|x| walk(tt, tgl, x)),
851	                                    Doc::line(),
852	                                )
853	                                .nest(1)
854	                                .group(),
855	                            )
856	                        })
857	                        .append(RcDoc::text("]"))
858	                } else if children.is_empty() {
859	                    RcDoc::as_string(current)
860	                } else {
861	                    RcDoc::text("(")
862	                        .append(RcDoc::as_string(current))
863	                        .append(RcDoc::text(" "))
864	                        .append(
865	                            RcDoc::intersperse(
866	                                children.iter().map(|x| walk(tt, tgl, x)),
867	                                Doc::line(),
868	                            )
869	                            .nest(1)
870	                            .group(),
871	                        )
872	                        .append(RcDoc::text(")"))
873	                }
874	            } else {
875	                // This should be unreachable if the invariants are maintained:
876	                RcDoc::text("<ThreadTree corrupt, missing tid: ")
877	                    .append(RcDoc::as_string(current))
878	                    .append(RcDoc::text(">"))
879	            }
880	        }
881	
882	        let root = match self.root {
883	            None => return "[]".into(),
884	            Some(root) => root,
885	        };
886	
887	        let doc = walk(&self.tree, &self.thread_group_leaders, &root);
888	        let width = 100;
889	        let mut vec = Vec::new();
890	        doc.render(width, &mut vec).unwrap();
891	        String::from_utf8(vec).unwrap()
892	    }

920	    /// owner to the caller's own parent task; threads never enter this process

923	        &mut self,
924	        parent_dettid: DetTid,
925	        child_dettid: DetTid,
926	        is_group_leader: bool,
927	        clone_parent: bool,
928	        exit_signal: libc::c_int,

931	        if parent_dettid == child_dettid {
932	            self.add_edge(None, child_dettid);
933	        } else {
934	            self.add_edge(Some(parent_dettid), child_dettid);
935	        }
936	        if is_group_leader {
937	            self.thread_group_leaders.insert(child_dettid);
938	            self.thread_to_leader.insert(child_dettid, child_dettid);
939	            if parent_dettid == child_dettid {
940	                self.process_wait.insert(
941	                    child_dettid,
942	                    ProcessWaitMetadata {
943	                        wait_parent: None,
944	                        wait_owner: child_dettid,
945	                        exit_signal: libc::SIGCHLD,
946	                        process_group: child_dettid,
947	                        session: child_dettid,
948	                    },
949	                );
950	            } else {
951	                let parent_process = self
952	                    .thread_to_leader
953	                    .get(&parent_dettid)
954	                    .copied()
955	                    .expect("process child parent must have a thread-group leader");
956	                let parent_metadata = self.process_wait.get(&parent_process).copied().unwrap_or(
957	                    ProcessWaitMetadata {
958	                        wait_parent: None,
959	                        wait_owner: parent_dettid,
960	                        exit_signal: libc::SIGCHLD,
961	                        process_group: parent_process,
962	                        session: parent_process,
963	                    },
964	                );
965	                let (wait_parent, wait_owner) = if clone_parent {
966	                    (parent_metadata.wait_parent, parent_metadata.wait_owner)
967	                } else {
968	                    (Some(parent_process), parent_dettid)
969	                };
970	                if let Some(wait_parent) = wait_parent {
971	                    self.process_parent.insert(child_dettid, wait_parent);
972	                }
973	                self.process_wait.insert(
974	                    child_dettid,
975	                    ProcessWaitMetadata {
976	                        wait_parent,
977	                        wait_owner,
978	                        exit_signal,
979	                        process_group: parent_metadata.process_group,
980	                        session: parent_metadata.session,
981	                    },
982	                );
983	            }
984	        } else {
985	            let parent_leader: DetPid =
986	                    *self
987	                        .thread_to_leader
988	                        .get(&parent_dettid)
989	                        .unwrap_or_else(|| {
990	                            panic!("recv_create_child_thread: parent {} of child dtid {} does not exist in thread_to_leader map!",
991	                                   parent_dettid, child_dettid);
992	                        });

1028	    /// Return the set of thread IDs in the "same process" as me (same TGID), including
1029	    /// myself.
1030	    ///
1031	    /// Locks: takes scheduler lock.
1032	    pub fn my_thread_group(&mut self, me: &DetTid) -> Vec<DetTid> {
1033	        let root_tid: DetTid = if self.thread_group_leaders.contains(me) {
1034	            *me
1035	        } else {
1036	            *self
1037	                .thread_to_leader
1038	                .get(me)
1039	                .expect("thread must be in to_leader table")
1040	        };
1041	        let mut stack: Vec<DetTid> = vec![root_tid];
1042	        let mut acc: Vec<DetTid> = vec![];
1043	
1044	        while let Some(first) = stack.pop() {
1045	            if self.thread_group_leaders.contains(&first) && first != root_tid {
1046	                continue; // Stop traversal when we walk into child processes.
1047	            } else {
1048	                acc.push(first);
1049	            }
1050	            let children = self.get_children(&first);
1051	            stack.extend_from_slice(children);
1052	        }
1053	        assert!(acc.contains(me));
1054	        acc
1055	    }
1056	}

1067	/// A simple backoff strategy while we have any realtime/polling elements in the system.
1068	/// When all external polling is removed, we can remove this.
1069	struct Backoff {
1070	    count: u64,
1071	}
1072	
1073	impl Backoff {
1074	    fn new() -> Self {
1075	        Backoff { count: 0 }
1076	    }
1077	
1078	    async fn further(&mut self, blocking: bool) {
1079	        self.count += 1;
1080	        const YIELDS_FIRST: u64 = 10;
1081	        if blocking {
1082	            if self.count <= YIELDS_FIRST {
1083	                std::thread::yield_now();
1084	            } else {
1085	                let round = self.count - YIELDS_FIRST;
1086	                let micros = if round > 13 { 10_000 } else { 2 ^ round };
1087	                std::thread::sleep(Duration::from_micros(micros));
1088	            }
1089	        } else if self.count <= YIELDS_FIRST {
1090	            tokio::task::yield_now().await;
1091	        } else {
1092	            let round = self.count - YIELDS_FIRST;
1093	            let micros = if round > 13 { 10_000 } else { 2 ^ round };
1094	            tokio::time::sleep(Duration::from_micros(micros)).await;
1095	        }
1096	    }
1097	
1098	    fn reset(&mut self) {
1099	        self.count = 0;
1100	    }
1101	}

1123	async fn sched_loop_inner(
1124	    sched: Arc<Mutex<Scheduler>>,
1125	    timer: Arc<Mutex<GlobalTime>>,
1126	    blocking_backoff: bool,
1127	    observer: Option<SchedulerObserver>,
1128	) {
1129	    // The "daemon task starting up" INFO line is deliberately NOT emitted here.
1130	    //
1131	    // This body runs inside a `tokio::spawn`ed task (see
1132	    // `GlobalState::initialize`), so the moment it is first polled is
1133	    // unsynchronized with the spawning thread's continued bootstrap. That made
1134	    // the line race the root thread's `USER RAND` / `CHAOSRAND` seeding lines
1135	    // from `ThreadState::new`, and the L2 comparator reads the INFO stream as
1136	    // ordered evidence: the two runs were identical as multisets and differed
1137	    // only in this one line's position, which is a real `bitwise_parity: false`.
1138	    //
1139	    // The announcement is now emitted by whoever starts the daemon, in that
1140	    // thread's program order, so it is deterministically sequenced after
1141	    // `Scheduler::new`'s `SCHEDRAND` line and before the root `ThreadState`.
1142	    // That is the order the ptrace backend already produced reliably.
1143	    //
1144	    // The observer callback stays here, at the point the task genuinely begins
1145	    // executing, because it is a barrier signal for external backends and is
1146	    // not part of the compared log stream. Moving the log does not cost us the
1147	    // "it actually started" observation for the consumer that needs it.
1148	    if let Some(observer) = &observer {
1149	        observer("daemon task starting; waiting for guest thread");
1150	    }
1151	    let (iv, stop_after_iter) = {
1152	        // Block until queue is populated.
1153	        let sched = sched.lock().unwrap();
1154	        (sched.started_up.clone(), sched.stop_after_iter)
1155	    };
1156	    if until_backend_failure(&sched, iv.get()).await.is_err() {
1157	        return;
1158	    }
1159	    info!("[scheduler] guest in queue, scheduler proceeding..",);
1160	    if let Some(observer) = &observer {
1161	        observer("guest registered; deterministic scheduler proceeding");
1162	    }
1163	    let mut iter: u64 = 0;
1164	    // We keep track of whether the last turn was a SKIP:
1165	    let mut last_res = Err(SkipTurn);
1166	    let mut backoff = Backoff::new();
1167	    let mut observed_turn = false;
1168	
1169	    loop {
1170	        if sched.lock().unwrap().backend_failed() {
1171	            return;
1172	        }
1173	        // TODO (T137183027, T137184765): as part of the current strategy for blocking IO ops (see
1174	        // SPINNING below), we need to make sure that other threads can progress so we don't
1175	        // busy-wait too tightly.
1176	        if last_res.is_err() {
1177	            backoff.further(blocking_backoff).await;
1178	        } else {
1179	            backoff.reset();
1180	        }
1181	
1182	        trace!("[scheduler] loop iteration {}", iter);
1183	        if stop_after_iter.is_some() && iter > stop_after_iter.unwrap() {
1184	            let sched = sched.lock().unwrap();
1185	            tracing::warn!(
1186	                "[scheduler] Early exit during sched loop iteration {} due to --stop-after-iter.  Summary:\n\n{}",
1187	                iter,
1188	                sched.full_summary()
1189	            );
1190	            immediate_fatal_exit(); // We don't want a backtrace of this thread.
1191	        }
1192	        iter += 1;
1193	
1194	        // If there are NO threads left in the system, then we're truly done:
1195	        {
1196	            let sched = sched.lock().unwrap();
1197	            if sched.backend_failed() {
1198	                return;
1199	            }
1200	            if sched.run_queue.is_empty()
1201	                && sched.blocked.is_empty()
1202	                && sched.pending_physical_process_exits.is_empty()
1203	                && sched.pending_run_queue_admissions.is_empty()
1204	                && sched.pending_run_queue_removals.is_empty()
1205	            {
1206	                info!("[scheduler] run queue empty, exiting sched_loop.");
1207	                if let Some(observer) = &observer {
1208	                    observer("run queue empty; scheduler completed");
1209	                }
1210	                return;
1211	            } else if let Some(stop) = sched.stop_after_turn
1212	                && sched.turn > stop
1213	            {
1214	                tracing::warn!(
1215	                    "[scheduler] Early exit during turn {} due to --stop-after-turn.  Summary:\n\n{}",
1216	                    sched.turn,
1217	                    sched.full_summary()
1218	                );
1219	                immediate_fatal_exit(); // We don't want a backtrace of this thread.
1220	            }
1221	        }
1222	
1223	        // Otherwise we trust the turn function to either choose a runnable thread or wait
1224	        // until something blocked is ready to run again.
1225	        last_res = do_a_turn_blocking(sched.clone(), timer.clone(), &last_res).await;
1226	
1227	        // A terminal deadlock ends the run here, alongside the two
1228	        // `--stop-after-*` exits above, rather than by panicking out of the
1229	        // scheduler task (see `report_terminal_deadlock`).
1230	        //
1231	        // Printed with `eprintln!` rather than `tracing::error!` on purpose: the
1232	        // tracing writer prefixes a real wall-clock timestamp, and this report
1233	        // is required to be byte-identical across runs of the same program.
1234	        if let Some(report) = sched.lock().unwrap().take_terminal_deadlock() {
1235	            eprintln!("{}", report);
1236	            immediate_fatal_exit(); // We don't want a backtrace of this thread.
1237	        }
1238	
1239	        if last_res.is_ok() && !observed_turn {
1240	            if let Some(observer) = &observer {
1241	                observer("completed a deterministic scheduling turn");
1242	            }
1243	            observed_turn = true;
1244	        }
1245	    }
1246	}

1261	/// Wait without manufacturing a normal scheduler request or response. The
1262	/// caller must check the terminal state again under the mutex before mutation.
1263	async fn until_backend_failure<T>(
1264	    sched: &Arc<Mutex<Scheduler>>,
1265	    wait: impl std::future::Future<Output = T>,
1266	) -> Result<T, SkipTurn> {
1267	    let failure = {
1268	        let sched = sched.lock().unwrap();
1269	        if sched.backend_failed() {
1270	            return Err(SkipTurn);
1271	        }
1272	        sched.backend_failure_waiter()
1273	    };
1274	    futures::pin_mut!(wait, failure);
1275	    match futures::future::select(failure, wait).await {
1276	        futures::future::Either::Left((notice, _)) => {
1277	            notice.expect("scheduler owns the failure sender until publication");
1278	            Err(SkipTurn)
1279	        }
1280	        futures::future::Either::Right((value, _)) => Ok(value),
1281	    }
1282	}

1284	/// Advance turn by 1 turn, blocking when necessary to make it happen.
1285	/// Return the outcome of the turn as well as which resources were used, if any.
1286	///
1287	/// WARNING: this is duplicated with the non-blocking `step` function below.
1288	/// TODO: this duplication is temporary and they should be either combined or one removed soon.
1289	async fn do_ordinary_turn_blocking(
1290	    sched: Arc<Mutex<Scheduler>>,
1291	    global_time: Arc<Mutex<GlobalTime>>,
1292	    last_turn: &Result<Resources, SkipTurn>,
1293	) -> Result<Resources, SkipTurn> {
1294	    // Loop until all threads are parked, then proceed:
1295	    //
1296	    // TODO: First, this check can move after step2, before we commit the action. Second,
1297	    // it can later grow more sophisticated to only check the completion of dependent
1298	    // actions, not all outsanding guest actions.
1299	    loop {
1300	        // We must read the queue carefully, because it can grow in the background
1301	        // everytime we await.  However, while it can *grow*, it cannot change order, as
1302	        // only the scheduler thread (us) actually rotates entries from the front to the back.
1303	        let req_ivar = {
1304	            let mut mg = sched.lock().unwrap();
1305	            if mg.backend_failed() {
1306	                return Err(SkipTurn);
1307	            }
1308	            let arc = global_time.clone();
1309	
1310	            let next_outstanding = mg.step1_check_quiescence(&arc, last_turn);
1311	            match next_outstanding {
1312	                None => {
1313	                    trace!("Scheduler observed full quiescense, proceeding...");
1314	                    break;
1315	                }
1316	                Some(iv) => iv.clone(),
1317	            }
1318	        };
1319	        trace!("Scheduler wait for full quiescense, on {}...", req_ivar);
1320	        let _ = until_backend_failure(&sched, req_ivar).await?;
1321	    }
1322	
1323	    // Here we copy some information while holding the sched lock, and then release it so
1324	    // we can `.await` below:
1325	    let (next_dtid, req, resp) = {
1326	        let mut sched = sched.lock().unwrap();
1327	        if sched.backend_failed() {
1328	            return Err(SkipTurn);
1329	        }
1330	        sched.step2_process_blocked(&global_time)?;
1331	        sched.step3_peek().ok_or(SkipTurn)?
1332	    };
1333	
1334	    finish_selected_turn(sched, global_time, next_dtid, req, resp).await
1335	}

1337	pub async fn do_a_turn_blocking(
1338	    sched: Arc<Mutex<Scheduler>>,
1339	    global_time: Arc<Mutex<GlobalTime>>,
1340	    last_turn: &Result<Resources, SkipTurn>,
1341	) -> Result<Resources, SkipTurn> {
1342	    let controlled = sched.lock().unwrap().kvm_shared_dequeue_timers;
1343	    if !controlled {
1344	        return do_ordinary_turn_blocking(sched, global_time, last_turn).await;
1345	    }
1346	    let result = async {
1347	        // A control pause retains both its maintenance position and the unpaid
1348	        // obligation of the preceding real turn. Transport messages never pay it.
1349	        enum Action {
1350	            Wait {
1351	                request: Option<Ivar<SchedRequest>>,
1352	                control: Ivar<()>,
1353	                barrier: bool,
1354	            },
1355	            Select(DetTid, Ivar<SchedRequest>, Ivar<SchedResponse>),
1356	        }
1357	        let mut charged = false;
1358	        let mut refresh = false;
1359	        let mut maintenance = 0;
1360	        // The reference admits one due event before a selection. Control
1361	        // callbacks may refresh observed time, but must not spend that event
1362	        // budget again and reverse ordinary sleepers' queue-front order.
1363	        let mut timed_event_processed = false;
1364	        let mut empty_queue_skip = false;
1365	        loop {
1366	            signal_control::flush_signal_failures(&sched);
1367	            let action = {
1368	                let mut state = sched.lock().unwrap();
1369	                state.drain_control_intents();
1370	                if state.backend_failed() {
1371	                    return Err(SkipTurn);
1372	                }
1373	                let barrier = state.control_barrier();
1374	                if empty_queue_skip && !barrier {
1375	                    return Err(SkipTurn);
1376	                }
1377	                let request = state.are_all_quiesced();
1378	                if !barrier && request.is_none() {
1379	                    if !charged {

1	# PROJECT VISION — Coordinator Prime Directive
2	
3	**Purpose:** This is the standing directive for the dev-hermit coordinator. Re-read every 1-2 hours. It prevents drift, lost inertia, and distraction.
4	
5	## Mission
6	
7	Aggressively drive hermit toward its final form: a production-grade deterministic execution engine with multiple backends (ptrace, KVM, Liteinst first party, plus DBT, e9patch, sabre with 3rd party deps) that all produce identical behavior/logs/memory, i.e. PARITY, plus record/replay and chaos concurrency testing that is equally broadly-compatible with arbitrary guest programs.
8	
9	Don't forget your general princples around CLEAR and SPECIFIC communication (which programs ran what under what mode and which branch/version was experimented with?) and presenting EVIDENCE for claims, including wherever possible reproducer commands.
10	
11	## Applications
12	
13	All the internal implementation priorities below are focused on making hermit USEFUL on real applications, which currently include but are not limited to:
14	
15	 - Linux kernel (and driver, and file system) concurrency testing and debugging inside QEMU inside hermit. Example milestones include getting our Linux demos running on non-ptrace hermit backends with improved performance.
16	 - Reproducible builds: including unblocking a watertight content addressable store mode for Nix, and being adoption ready for the Debian Reproducible Builds project or other distros or package managers.  Example milestones include enabling parallelism in detcore so `make -j` can use real parallelism, ideally with minimal determinism overhead from an efficient (non-ptrace) Reverie backend.
17	 - Record/replay debugging of userspace apps a la Mozilla rr. Example milestones include recording firefox (controlled by playwright) like rr originally targetted.
18	
19	## Priorities
20	
21	We expand compatibility across a set of tracked programs, most of which are part of the CI suite (but we can do periodic testing outside of it). We have have a common denominator for ALL tests in our CI manifests, and terminology for "cells" (mode x backend x test) which should monotonically increase in total coverage, both for DETERMINISM and for the stronger PARITY level of achievement (i.e. backend X runs program Y deterministically AND bitwise identical to the ptrace reference impl).
22	
23	Hermit has a series of modes:
24	
25	0. **Smoke test** -- running through hermit at all, with enforcement less than --strict, is a good first step on a new application but is not something we use as a goal (though "minimal dosing" of hermit is useful for reproducible builds).
26	1. **Rock-solid hermit run** — expand --strict --verify compatibility envelope to arbitrary programs across many classes.
27	2. **Record/replay** — expand R/R to match --verify coverage (e.g. fix pipe deadlocks), perodically compare against mature "rr"
28	3. Chaos mode and hermit analyze for concurency testing and race localization.
29	
30	Then the above modes can run in each of the backends, with running in non-ptrace backends being the expanding frontier that we need to drive.
31	
32	## Mode Expansion Mandate
33	
34	Every mode must catch up to the one before it, and advanced, higher-perf backends must catch up with the reference one:
35	- Example: 300 programs in --strict --verify → same 300 in record/replay → same in DBT → same in KVM, and the denominator are always the e2e tests we planned in the overhaul.
36	- There is NO stopping while trailing modes are weaker
37	- Always add NEW programs to coverage even as trailing modes catch up
38	
39	Agents will constantly try to put up fake results that mislead you, where they have mocked up something partial that is NOT the real thing we want. You must be skeptical and you must ask questions and check assumptions, and ask for evidence and details on provenance and what's ACTUALLY running.
40	
41	## Operations and Regulation
42	
43	1. **Land PRs, keep main green, zero compile warnings**
44	2. **Monitor resources** - check frequently CPU disk, memory, etc and do not allow too many local validates or zombie processes, or out of control experiments, to take down the box.
45	3. **Keep agent fleet busy** You are driving autonomously at FULL SPEED, with 10-15 agents busy on this big dev box. You have multiple lines of P0 work and massive open-ended backlogs. Pre-generate parallel work in the task graph.
46	4. **Check CI health and ci-runner queue depth**, make sure we are not overwhelming CI and that it is healthy and green. Get as close to zero open PRs as you can, and not PRs than agents. Cancellation policy should mean not too many jobs outstanding and we can always supplement CI with local `scripts/validate.rs` / locally-validated receipt protocol. We can have separate policies for github-hosted actions and self-hosted ones but BOTH SHOULD ALWAYS HAVE RECENT GREEN RESULTS, and if not that is a P0 crisis to fix.
47	5. **Clean repo state** — minimal open PRs, branches deleted after merge, `git status` clean in both parent and hermit/reverie checkouts
48	
49	## Failure Modes to Avoid
50	
51	1. **Lost inertia:** "0 busy, 0 ready" is a P0 alarm, not "nothing to do." Generate work immediately.
52	2. **Heartbeat/fleet-monitor paused:** NEVER pause these workflows. They are mission-critical safety nets.
53	3. **Agent exhaustion:** Try to /compact agents before they run out of context, but when agents hit 100% context, spawn fresh ones immediately at `~/work/dev-hermit/hermit`. Don't let all agents exhaust simultaneously.
54	4. **Empty task pipeline:** Always have 10+ tasks queued ahead of current execution. Pre-generate work.
55	5. **Overstating progress:** "14/14 R/R tests pass" means nothing if --verify has 300 programs. Measure gaps, not victories.
56	6. **Calling something a backend when it isn't:** A backend loads Detcore as Tool. One shared copy of the code. Prototypes and stubs are NOT backends.
57	7. **Forgetting cleanup:** Branch hygiene, repo organization, stale worktrees — these rot if ignored.
58	8. **Waiting for user review:** Do own review iterations. Don't block on human review. Use adversarial agent review.
59	9. **Single-threaded thinking:** Debugging is parallelizable. Burst agents for root-causing. Implementation can parallelize across subsystems.
60	10. **Stale context reuse:** Restart agents when their context is stale or full. Fresh agents with clear tasks beat exhausted agents with fuzzy context.
61	11. **Broken CI, agents ignoring it:** CI is red but agents locally validate to land, not fixing the problem.
62	
63	## Autonomous Operation Protocol
64	
65	- **Generate work continuously.** Every agent completion should trigger: check results → create downstream tasks → assign next work.
66	- **Own PR iterations.** Adversarial review by different agent, fix issues, land. Don't wait.
67	- **Report precisely, with provenance.** State WHERE (main, feature branch, PR #N). Qualify results (L0/L1/L2). Never unqualified "passing."
68	- **Keep 10+ agents busy** at all times. If fewer are busy, spawn or generate work.
69	- **Path validation before spawn.** Check cwd exists before spawning agents.
70	- **Commit immediately, push immediately.** No work left uncommitted or unpushed.
71	
72	## Architecture North Stars
73	
74	### Hermit run
75	
76	Runs essentially arbitrary user space Linux programs under --strict --verify with perfect deterministic execution. This includes our deep workstream on emulating the Linux kernel under QEMU.
77	
78	Allows advanced chaos mode which perturbs program schedule orders and is compatible with all programs that normal --strict --verify runs on.
79	
80	### Hermit record / replay
81	
82	Works for everything rr does. Eventually is configurable from an rr-like mode to a `hermit run` mode that ONLY records external communication at the container boundary (and optionally file system boundary).
83	
84	### Drive Reverie BACKENDS
85	
86	Keep one fixed-purpose agent for each backend: "hermit-kvm", "hermit-dbi", "hermit-sabre", "hermit-liteinst", "hermit-e9patch".  Each will drive forward to have a complete and correct Reverie backend (working for arbitrary Reverie tools) plus hermit/detcore integration eventually supporting ALL the same guest programs deterministically as hermit/ptrace.
87	
88	### KVM Backend
89	Highest priority, will probably be our flagship backend.
90	```
91	hermit-cli → Detcore<KvmGuest> → KVM (gvisor model)
92	  Similar to gvisor (Go program as kernel, trap all syscalls in userspace) but with Detcore tool as the "operating system".
93	  NO hacks or temporary proof-of-concepts. Fully runs all hermit --strict --verify that ptrace can.
94	```
95	### LiteInst Backend
96	
97	Aside from KVM and ptrace, ALL other binary patching/instrumentation backends keep the Reverie local tool INSIDE the guest address space (communicating to the global state through RPC that shares code between reverie-liteinst, reverie-dbt, reverie-sabre, reverie-e9patch).
98	
99	Based on my instruction punning invention and our new reimplemntation (liteinst2), which provides DYNAMIC hooking of arbitrary instructions.
100	In this backend, we trap nondeterministic instructions (syscalls/cpuid/rdtsc/rdrand/etc) but on the first trap we patch them to hook directly into the guest.
101	
102	Our plan is to use LD_PRELOAD to infect the guest (and its children) and remove the need for ptrace as much as possible, but resort to a ptrace supervisor as a backup if there is a corner case we cannot handle.
103	
104	### DBT Backend
105	Dynamic Binary Translation based on DynamoRIO. This should be foolproof at catching nondeterministic instructions, and has the benefit that it can build branch-counting directly in, avoiding the problem of massive skid on PMU retired branch conditional timers. But it will probably fail on self-modifying code, e.g JVM JITs or QEMU TCG.
106	
107	```
108	hermit-cli → Detcore<DbtGuest> → DynamoRIO
109	  NO hacks or temporary proof-of-concepts. Fully runs all hermit --strict --verify that ptrace can.
110	```
111	
112	### Sabre Backend
113	Another binary patching backend, but at startup time it scans all application code.  With this one we use ptrace + sabre and hew closer to the design of the ptrace backend but try to optimize how many nondet instructions avoid traps.  However, ptrace needs to be able to redirect trapped instructions to in-guest handlers because the Reverie tool state lives in guest address spaces.
114	
115	### e9patch Backend
116	Based on instruction punning like LiteInst but at startup time.  We pair this with our own scanning for nondet instructions (CFG reconstruction), very similar to Sabre. But we try to share the same LD_PRELOAD injection method making this a close counterpart to the LiteInst backend.
117	
118	### Done = Identical (Parity)
119	A backend is done when ALL programs produce bitwise-identical output across all hermit reverie backends (ptrace/KVM/Liteinst/etc). Same memory hashes, same guest output, same exit codes.

1	# Hermit v2 Roadmap
2	
3	Status: consolidated research and execution plan, 2026-07-21
4	
5	This document consolidates the Hermit and Reverie research recorded in the
6	`dev-hermit` task graph. It describes the product goal, the measured current
7	state, the major technical choices, and a dependency-ordered implementation
8	plan.
9	
10	## Executive summary
11	
12	Hermit v2 should become a robust deterministic execution engine for real Linux
13	binaries, with reproducible run/record/replay, schedule stress and search, and
14	a lower-overhead execution backend. The longer-term Linux-kernel milestone is
15	to run a pinned QEMU/TCG VM under Hermit, combine it with an in-guest race
16	oracle, and make the host-side QEMU schedule a replayable input.
17	
18	The project has a functioning base, but several historical status claims need
19	qualification:
20	
21	- The current fork builds and its primary local validation passes. A current
22	  inventory on `main` counted 175 named Cargo cases: 173 pass and two doctests
23	  are ignored. The often-repeated "300+ ported tests" describes work attempted
24	  across branches and worktrees, not the authoritative coverage on `main`.
25	- Hosted CI is healthy. The self-hosted runner executes CPUID and PMU checks,
26	  but full Hermit integration coverage is not green: nested network namespace
27	  setup needs a `sysfs` mount that fails in the current runner container.
28	  Running the runner privileged or outside its container is the proven fix.
29	- Event-level schedule search works end to end. It localized both
30	  `hello_race` and `racewrite_nostdlib` to source lines with stack traces.
31	  Replay jitter, event alignment, disabled sub-event refinement, and weak
32	  endpoint validation prevent calling it a supported general feature yet.
33	- The restored SaBRe stack is a real runnable prototype, not just source
34	  archaeology. Its narrow raw-syscall path was about 13x faster than ptrace,
35	  but its in-process signal, thread, lifecycle, and API semantics remain the
36	  dominant risk. A useful synchronous backend is estimated at 5-8 weeks;
37	  broad parity is 12-20+ weeks with architectural caveats.
38	- DynamoRIO is the strongest maintained binary-instrumentation alternative.
39	  It deserves a time-boxed proof of concept before SaBRe becomes a strategic
40	  dependency.
41	- A `reverie-kvm` protocol skeleton exists and passes five unit tests, but it
42	  intentionally returns `SentryBridgeNotImplemented`. A production KVM path
43	  means integrating with a Linux ABI provider such as gVisor's Sentry, not
44	  merely issuing KVM ioctls. The estimate is 4-6 engineer-months for an MVP and
45	  9-15 engineer-months for broad parity and hardening.
46	- QEMU/TCG can boot under a deliberately relaxed Hermit configuration. Full
47	  deterministic mode is currently too slow and semantically incomplete. The
48	  measured boot uses 147,679 syscalls across 54 names; `ppoll`, futex timeout
49	  correctness, vectored I/O, inherited-file handling, and external helper
50	  state are the main path to a strict deterministic boot.
51	
52	The recommended order is: restore trustworthy green gates, fix real-binary
53	correctness and precise-PMU overhead, harden schedule search, then advance two
54	parallel bets - a measured fast-backend prototype and deterministic QEMU/TCG.
55	Do not begin the long KVM/Sentry program or open-ended kernel fuzzing until
56	those gates provide stable evidence.
57	
58	## Vision and success criteria
59	
60	Hermit v2 is a deterministic execution platform for arbitrary Linux ELF
61	binaries and their process trees. Its product capabilities are:
62	
63	1. Run arbitrary dynamically linked, multithreaded, signal-heavy programs with
64	   explicit boundaries for filesystem, network, and external inputs.
65	2. Record and replay executions faithfully, with actionable divergence
66	   diagnostics rather than hangs or opaque panics.
67	3. Explore scheduling interleavings in chaos mode and reproduce a selected
68	   outcome by seed and artifacts.
69	4. Search between passing and failing schedules, reduce the difference to a
70	   validated event ordering, and report stack/source context.
71	5. Provide at least one production-quality backend that avoids ptrace's
72	   syscall-stop cost while retaining a documented Reverie capability subset.
73	6. Allow non-communicating processes to run in parallel without abandoning the
74	   deterministic model.
75	7. Maintain comprehensive, resource-bounded CI for ordinary, PMU-dependent,
76	   namespace-dependent, record/replay, and schedule-search behavior.
77	
78	The QEMU/Linux milestone is a downstream application of those capabilities:
79	a pinned, immutable Linux VM under QEMU/TCG whose workload, oracle output, and
80	Hermit schedule can be replayed and reduced. Hermit supplies schedule control,
81	not the kernel race oracle; KCSAN, KASAN, LOCKDEP, panic/hang detection, or a
82	workload invariant must supply the failure predicate.
83	
84	## Current state
85	
86	### Repository, build, and workflow
87	
88	- `rrnewton/hermit` is the maintained product fork. Cargo is the primary
89	  external build, and `scripts/validate.rs` covers workspace build/tests, clippy,
90	  formatting, docs, and the evolving integration gates.
91	- `dev-hermit` is the parent harness. It pins Hermit and Reverie, owns durable
92	  research and experiments, and provides isolated paired worktrees.
93	- The fbsource Buck tree remains valuable as the historical test inventory. It
94	  has 745 test rules and builds fully, but a monolithic run is not a useful
95	  presubmit: the last full audit reported 520 passes, 36 failures, 301
96	  timeouts, and one omission, with extensive oversubscription effects.
97	
98	### Test coverage
99	
100	The authoritative current-main audit found:
101	
102	| Surface | Current evidence | Interpretation |
103	| --- | --- | --- |
104	| Cargo named cases | 175 | 173 pass; two Hermit doctests ignored |
105	| Buck test rules | 745 | 744 executable targets plus one suite |
106	| Buck hardware split | 205 no-hardware, 538 PMU-only, 1 PMU+CPUID | Most historical matrix coverage needs the self-hosted lane |
107	| Schedule search | Two real E2E workloads pass locally | Not yet a reliable general algorithm or consistently landed CI gate |
108	| Arbitrary binaries | Simple tools pass; medium/complex failures filed | Current support is useful but not yet "arbitrary" |
109	
110	Some test-port work exists only on external branches or unreachable/stashed
111	worktree commits. It must be recovered, reviewed, and landed before being
112	counted. In particular, the historical wave-two claim cannot be used as a
113	current-main denominator. The coverage program should report exact tests at an
114	exact SHA and separate ordinary, PMU, namespace, quarantined, and unlanded
115	cases.
116	
117	### Continuous integration
118	
119	The CI architecture is correct in principle:
120	
121	- GitHub-hosted Linux runs ordinary build, tests, clippy, formatting, and docs.
122	- A self-hosted runner supplies CPUID and PMU hardware coverage.
123	- Namespace and schedule-search tests belong on the self-hosted lane.
124	
125	The remaining infrastructure blocker is deeper than the original user/mount
126	namespace probe. Full Hermit mode also creates a network namespace and mounts
127	`sysfs`. In a rootless Podman reproduction, relaxing seccomp, unmasking system
128	paths, and adding `SYS_ADMIN`/`NET_ADMIN` still failed that mount; privileged
129	mode passed. Until the runner is privileged or moved outside the container,
130	the full `cargo test -p hermit` and schedule-search gates are not trustworthy
131	CI signals. A green fallback that runs only library/binary tests must not be
132	reported as full integration coverage.
133	
134	### Arbitrary binary support
135	
136	The current compatibility audit on Hermit `74324fff` found:
137	
138	| Tier | Works | Fails or remains limited |
139	| --- | --- | --- |
140	| Simple | `ls`, `cat`, `echo`, `grep`, `sed`, `awk` in run and record/verify; output matched native | Host fixture paths require explicit `--bind`, by design |
141	| Medium | GCC compile, system Git, Python file/hash/JSON/subprocess under `run` | Record/replay divergence; `ioctl(FIOCLEX)` missing; site Git/Python wrappers hang on `CLONE_VFORK` |
142	| Complex | Simple pipeline under `run` | rustup proxy FD tracking, direct Cargo/Make `CLONE_VFORK`, pipeline replay and child cleanup |
143	| Stress | `curl --network=host`; 4-thread/400-signal test in run and record/verify | blocking connect returns `EINPROGRESS`; external inputs remain nondeterministic |
144	
145	The minimized failure families are tracked as upstream issues #76 through #80:
146	process creation/cleanup, descriptor tracking, recorder ioctl coverage,
147	blocking network semantics, and multiprocess replay/cleanup.
148	
149	## Backend strategy
150	
151	### Ptrace baseline and performance
152	
153	Optimized default-mode measurements on an AMD EPYC host show why backend and
154	timer work must be treated separately:
155	
156	| Workload | Native | `hermit run` | Run overhead | `hermit record` | Record overhead |
157	| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
158	| `/bin/true`, 32 syscalls | 0.000784 s | 0.009830 s | 12.54x | 0.021831 s | 27.85x |
159	| CPU-only, 100M iterations | 0.236879 s | 9.409876 s | 39.72x | 9.541134 s | 40.28x |
160	| 30,032 syscalls | 0.083166 s | 1.751327 s | 21.06x | 1.349976 s | 16.23x |
161	| 256 thread create/join | 0.008435 s | 1.209288 s | 143.37x | 0.940607 s | 111.51x |
162	
163	Minimal ptrace with precise preemption disabled was still 10.98x on the
164	syscall workload and 9.76x on the thread workload, about 27.6 microseconds per
165	censused syscall and 0.289 ms per created thread. Those numbers are the target
166	for a faster syscall backend.
167	
168	The 40x CPU-only result is not syscall interception. Precise retired
169	conditional branch (RCB) preemption produced about 1.9 million context
170	switches; disabling preemption or using imprecise timers reduced the workload
171	to about 1.03x native. The AMD family 0x19 skid margin is 10,000, compared with
172	100 on Intel in the current model, creating a long single-step tail. Fast
173	syscall interception will not fix this. Timer calibration/algorithm work is an
174	independent P0 performance stream.
175	
176	### SaBRe
177	
178	What works now:
179	
180	- The historical nine-package stack was restored.
181	- Upstream SaBRe `05816ee` builds; 69 tests pass unmodified, three are
182	  unsupported, and three portability failures pass with scratch-only fixes.
183	- Vendored plugin API sources restore linking; `reverie-sabre` passes 17/17
184	  unit tests.
185	- `riptrace` loads its plugin and traces `/bin/true`, `/bin/echo`, exec,
186	  fork/wait, exit-status propagation, and summary counting.
187	- A narrow, single-threaded 200,000-`getpid` probe took about 0.32-0.33 s under
188	  SaBRe versus 4.13-4.45 s under ptrace, roughly 13x faster. This is directional
189	  evidence, not a general workload claim.
190	
191	What blocks production use:
192	
193	- SaBRe has a separate synchronous in-process `Tool` API, not the shared async
194	  Reverie `Tool`/`Guest` contract.
195	- Signal handlers, TLS/guard state, bounded queues, `rt_sigaction`, and signal
196	  replacement/suppression are incomplete. A Python-class workload exposed
197	  guard and signal-queue failures during parity research.
198	- Fork/clone/vfork/clone3/exec lifecycle continuity, parent-aware state, abrupt
199	  exits, protected FDs, registers, stack allocation, backtraces, PMU timers,
200	  CPUID, and RDTSCP are incomplete or absent.
201	- Static rewriting does not cover every static, JIT, self-modifying, or
202	  dynamically generated syscall path. In-process instrumentation shares the
203	  guest's failure domain.
204	- Upstream is dormant: last push in 2022, no releases, no active successor,
205	  concentrated historical ownership, and GPL-3.0-or-later constraints.
206	
207	The runtime-stabilization branch has fixed the exit-timeout direction, an exit
208	race, queue saturation behavior, guarded signal callbacks, and part of SIGCHLD
209	handling. It is paused for the Reverie fork migration; `rt_sigaction`
210	virtualization, conformance gates, documentation, and verification remain.
211	
212	Recommended SaBRe boundary:
213	
214	- First deliver an explicit synchronous, syscall-centric backend extension.
215	- Do not change shared Reverie core abstractions merely to claim parity.
216	- Require common ptrace/SaBRe conformance workloads before promoting a
217	  capability.
218	- Budget 5-8 weeks for a credible x86-64 synchronous backend after the initial
219	  gate, and 12-20+ weeks for broad behavioral parity. Exact async callbacks,
220	  signal control, abrupt exits, unrewritten code, and aarch64 remain separate
221	  risks.
222	
223	### DynamoRIO and other instrumentation choices
224	
225	DynamoRIO is the strongest maintained alternative. Its active BSD core has
226	direct pre/post syscall callbacks, filtering, argument/number/result mutation,
227	suppression, and repeated injection. It handles translated/generated code and
228	has an active Rust wrapper. Its main risks are whole-process DBI overhead,
229	synchronous/no-std callbacks, and bridging safely to async tool logic.
230	
231	Run a time-boxed DynamoRIO proof of concept before selecting SaBRe as the
232	default fast backend. The acceptance suite must cover modify/suppress/inject,
233	clone/fork/vfork/exec, signals/EINTR, static and dynamic programs, JIT syscall
234	instructions, guest memory, and synchronous-to-async reentrancy. Benchmark an
235	empty client, a no-subscription client, and subscribed callbacks against
236	native, ptrace, and the SaBRe raw-syscall probe.
237	
238	Other findings:
239	
240	- Linux Syscall User Dispatch is the strongest purpose-built non-DBI primitive
241	  for a custom backend, especially as a fallback for missed/JIT syscalls. It
242	  requires per-thread setup and difficult signal/alt-stack/exec/clone handling.
243	- Frida and QBDI are active but require substantial custom syscall semantics.
244	- Intel Pin is proprietary. E9Patch is GPL and lacks complete dynamic/JIT
245	  lifecycle coverage. zpoline's page-zero/SELinux requirements rule it out as
246	  the production default. Pure eBPF cannot implement Reverie's replace,
247	  injection, memory, lifecycle, and signal contract.
248	
249	### KVM backend
250	
251	The KVM design's central result is that KVM provides an execution boundary,
252	not a Linux syscall implementation. gVisor runs application code at guest ring
253	3 and routes `SYSCALL` into Sentry code at guest ring 0; the Sentry implements
254	Linux process, memory, signal, futex, and syscall behavior.
255	
256	The proposed architecture is a versioned Sentry bridge plus a Rust
257	`reverie-kvm` frontend. The Rust side owns tools and exposes `Guest`; the Sentry
258	owns virtual Linux tasks and publishes syscall, signal, thread, exec, and exit
259	events. A standalone Rust KVM loop would amount to building another Linux ABI
260	and is not the smaller option.
261	
262	Current implementation evidence is deliberately modest: a 310-line protocol
263	skeleton negotiates version, architecture, capabilities, and message bounds;
264	it passes `cargo check`, five unit tests, formatting, and diff checks. The
265	actual Sentry bridge is unimplemented. Retain the existing estimate of 4-6
266	engineer-months for an x86-64 MVP and 9-15 engineer-months for parity and
267	hardening. Start only after workload and backend benchmarks justify that
268	investment.
269	
270	## Schedule search and concurrency testing
271	
272	### What works
273	
274	The existing `hermit analyze` event-level search is operational:
275	
276	- `hello_race` started 6,088,241 adjacent swaps apart, converged to one event
277	  pair in 22 passes, emitted both stacks, and localized
278	  `flaky-tests/hello_race.rs:37`.
279	- `racewrite_nostdlib` converged in six passes with zero desynchronizations,
280	  isolated adjacent write posthooks, and localized
281	  `tests/c/simple/racewrite_nostdlib.c:35`.
282	- Edit-distance tests pass 22/22, schedule-search unit tests pass 3/3, and the
283	  CLI builds and exposes `analyze`.
284	
285	The algorithm records normalized schedule-event blocks, constructs an
286	adjacent-swap path between opposite-outcome schedules, executes a midpoint,
287	and replaces one endpoint until the boundary is one swap apart. Precise PMU
288	RCB timers enforce branch blocks, and the final runs capture stacks. This is a
289	linear-path boundary search, not exhaustive schedule enumeration or direct
290	memory-race localization.
291	
292	### Known limitations
293	
294	- Replay jitter can label a requested midpoint with the outcome of a different
295	  realized schedule and can move outside the intended interval.
296	- `swap_distance == 1` does not prove that only one event differs; insertions
297	  and deletions may remain. Greedy exact-block matching is weak for loops and
298	  split RCB blocks.
299	- Partial branch-count consumption, blocked-thread rules, syscall-prehook
300	  switching, and robust resynchronization are incomplete.
301	- Advertised explicit endpoint schedule inputs are unimplemented.
302	- Branch-level `sub_event_search` has been disabled since the original public
303	  history. Its bounds, applicability, jitter, and final A/B validation are not
304	  safe enough to enable.
305	- No stability sampling separates a deterministic ordering violation from
306	  residual nondeterminism. Current events cannot localize inside branch-free
307	  instruction regions or identify the actual racing load/store.
308	
309	The research estimate is 4-6 weeks for a credible x86-64 PMU-backed MVP and
310	8-12 weeks for a supported feature. Exact memory-access localization is a
311	separate instrumentation project.
312	
313	### Chaos stress results
314	
315	Chaos already exposes logical ordering bugs across thread counts. Ten-seed
316	matrices found lost atomic updates, publish-ordering errors, missing barriers,
317	producer/consumer ordering bugs, and lost condvar wakeups at varying rates.
318	`hello_race` failed 5/20 seeds; `hello_race_mini` failed 11/20. An imprecise
319	timer profile found `cas_sequence_easy` 31/100 times and reproduced seed 2 in
320	5/5 attempts, while precise discovery was impractically slow.
321	
322	Two boundaries matter:
323	
324	- The current stress wrapper can falsely skip all PMU tests because it searches
325	  modern `perf list` output for the obsolete phrase `Hardware event` (issue
326	  #82). This must be fixed before treating the gate as evidence.
327	- Serialized guest threads do not simulate weak memory. A relaxed-atomic
328	  store-buffer outcome occurred natively but 0/40 times under Hermit chaos.
329	  Hermit is best at logical ordering, lifetime, locking, and filesystem
330	  invariants, not genuine simultaneous weak-memory behavior.
331	
332	## QEMU and Linux-kernel milestone
333	
334	### Measured QEMU surface
335	
336	The validated QEMU 10.1.0 TCG boot made 147,679 calls across 54 syscall names.
337	The dominant calls were futex (62,456), `ppoll` (33,589), write (22,390), read
338	(19,856), `writev` (2,889), `mprotect` (2,351), and `madvise` (2,003).
339	
340	Detcore has dedicated arms for 26 names representing 72.09% of calls, explicit
341	passthrough for 11 names representing 3.17%, and fallback behavior for 17 names
342	representing 24.73%. `ppoll` plus `writev` account for 99.87% of fallback call
343	volume. Dedicated dispatch is not the same as deterministic correctness:
344	
345	- `FUTEX_WAIT_BITSET|FUTEX_CLOCK_REALTIME` is treated as relative and has a
346	  nanosecond-conversion bug; QEMU used it 649 times.
347	- `ppoll` lacks scheduler and record/replay semantics.
348	- Vectored I/O lacks complete resource/nonblocking/replay behavior.
349	- `recvmsg` does not record control data or received FDs, which matters for the
350	  external vhost-user filesystem helper.
351	- `fcntl`, `mmap`, PID/TID/rseq, file metadata/offset calls, and JIT mapping
352	  behavior remain partial.
353	
354	KVM mode is not the first target. It made 54,981 ioctls, 83.6% of all calls;
355	deterministically modeling KVM fd state, `kvm_run` pages, guest memory effects,
356	interrupts, and VM/vCPU lifecycle is a months-scale architecture project.
357	
358	### Current execution result
359	
360	QEMU/TCG boots and exits successfully under Hermit when precise preemption,
361	thread sequentialization, time virtualization, metadata virtualization, and
362	CPUID virtualization are disabled. The same minimal boot can pass
363	`--panic-on-unsupported-syscalls`. This proves syscall interception reach, not
364	deterministic VM execution.
365	
366	Full deterministic mode remains non-viable today:
367	
368	- sequentialization causes extreme vCPU/I/O-thread slowdown;
369	- virtualized time causes guest TSC/APIC clock-skew warnings;
370	- precise preemption adds the measured CPU overhead;
371	- vng inherited-initrd fd handling and external helper/filesystem state need a
372	  reproducible launch model.
373	
374	### Kernel race-testing position
375	
376	Hermit should be presented as a schedule-control and replay layer, not as a
377	replacement for syzkaller or KCSAN and not as the first deterministic kernel
378	scheduler. Razzer, SKI, Snowboard, and KRACE already demonstrate directed or
379	systematic kernel concurrency testing.
380	
381	The defensible value is composability: hold a pinned QEMU/TCG image and guest
382	workload constant, make the host QEMU schedule a first-class replay artifact,
383	and compare passing/failing schedules with the existing order-search tooling.
384	Use guest KCSAN/KASAN/LOCKDEP/panic/invariants as the oracle and syzkaller or LTP
385	as workload generators. Start with known logical concurrency bugs and two TCG
386	vCPUs. Do not claim weak-memory, DMA, or real-parallel coverage.
387	
388	## Prioritized work
389	
390	The following table orders deliverables by dependency and risk. "Planning
391	estimate" means the range was synthesized from the research when no task had a
392	formal estimate.
393	
394	| Priority | Deliverable | Completion evidence | Estimate | Depends on |
395	| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
396	| P0 | Make self-hosted CI truthful and green | Privileged/outside-container runner passes user+pid+uts+mount+net with proc, sysfs, and bind mounts; full Hermit and PMU lanes pass | 0.5-1 day ops | Runner host access |
397	| P0 | Establish exact coverage ledger | Exact-SHA report for landed ordinary/PMU/namespace/quarantined tests; recover and review valuable unlanded ports | 3-5 days | Green CI lanes |
398	| P0 | Fix false PMU stress skip | Modern capability probe; issue #82 closed; at least one chaos workload demonstrably runs in CI | 1-2 days | Self-hosted runner |
399	| P0 | Fix precise-PMU CPU overhead | Calibrated AMD skid handling or bounded alternative; CPU benchmark substantially below 40x without losing replay guarantee | 1-3 weeks, planning estimate | Dedicated PMU benchmark host |
400	| P0 | Repair real-binary correctness | Minimized regressions for issues #76-#80 pass in run and record/replay | 3-6 weeks, planning estimate | Coverage ledger |
401	| P1 | Land schedule-search E2E gate | `hello_race` and `racewrite_nostdlib` bounded gates pass on self-hosted CI | 1-2 days | Truthful PMU/namespace CI |
402	| P1 | Schedule-search validity MVP | Realized-schedule validation, stable identities/alignment, endpoint invariants, bounded search, repeated predicates | 4-6 weeks | PMU overhead work and CI gate |
403	| P1 | Complete SaBRe runtime stabilization | Thread/signal/lifecycle conformance gates; no shared core API changes | 2-5 weeks | Reverie fork migration, preserved stash |
404	| P1 | Time-box DynamoRIO prototype | Required syscall semantics and lifecycle tests plus comparative benchmark | 2-3 weeks, planning estimate | Backend-neutral conformance harness |
405	| P1 | Select fast-backend product boundary | Evidence-based decision between synchronous SaBRe, DynamoRIO, or custom SUD/patching | 1 week decision gate | SaBRe and DynamoRIO results |
406	| P1 | Strict deterministic QEMU/TCG boot | `ppoll`, futex timeouts, vectored I/O, fd handoff, immutable launch inputs | 2-3 weeks | Real-binary correctness, PMU/time work |
407	| P1 | QEMU record/replay/verify | Stable replay including required fd/control-message state; repeated exact output | 4-6 weeks | Strict TCG boot |
408	| P2 | Supported schedule search | Sub-event refinement where applicable, stress, artifacts/UX, fork/exec/signal coverage | 8-12 weeks total | Validity MVP and fast/reliable replay |
409	| P2 | Kernel race feasibility demo | Known guest bug, stable oracle, reproducible seed, passing/failing schedule pair, reduced operation delta | 4-8 weeks, planning estimate | QEMU verify and schedule-search MVP |
410	| P2 | Useful synchronous fast backend | Ordinary syscall inspect/suppress/replace/inject, memory, state, lifecycle, conformance | 5-8 weeks for SaBRe path | Backend selection |
411	| P3 | Broad fast-backend parity | Signals, PMU, CPUID/RDTSCP, state, diagnostics, architecture decisions | 12-20+ weeks | Useful backend proven on workloads |
412	| P3 | gVisor/Sentry KVM backend MVP | Implement bridge behind current protocol skeleton and run selected tools | 4-6 engineer-months | Workload justification and dedicated team |
413	| P3 | KVM parity/hardening | Broader lifecycle, signals, performance, security, operational support | 9-15 engineer-months total | KVM MVP |
414	
415	## Dependencies and parallelism
416	
417	The critical dependency graph is:
418	
419	```text
420	truthful CI + exact coverage
421	  -> arbitrary-binary correctness
422	  -> stable run/record/replay
423	  -> schedule-search validity
424	  -> QEMU record/replay
425	  -> kernel race feasibility demo
426	
427	truthful CI + backend-neutral conformance
428	  -> SaBRe stabilization -----+
429	  -> DynamoRIO prototype -----+-> fast-backend selection
430	                                  -> useful backend
431	                                  -> process parallelism/parity
432	
433	PMU benchmark gate
434	  -> precise-preemption optimization
435	  -> practical schedule discovery and QEMU execution
436	
437	KVM/Sentry design + workload justification
438	  -> KVM bridge MVP
439	  -> parity/hardening
440	```
441	
442	Three workstreams can run in parallel after the P0 gate:
443	
444	1. Correctness and coverage: issues #76-#82, CI, port recovery, ordinary
445	   run/record/replay.
446	2. Performance and backends: precise PMU optimization, SaBRe stabilization,
447	   DynamoRIO proof of concept, common conformance benchmarks.
448	3. Schedule/QEMU: search validity work and strict TCG syscall/launch support.
449	
450	Integration checkpoints should occur at exact SHAs every one to two weeks.
451	Each checkpoint must publish test counts, benchmark commands, runner
452	capabilities, and known skips. Kernel experiments start only after the QEMU
453	verify checkpoint; KVM implementation starts only after a backend/workload
454	review explicitly funds the months-scale program.
455	
456	## Decision gates
457	
458	1. **CI gate:** no "green" claim while required namespace/PMU tests are skipped
459	   or the runner cannot execute full Hermit integration targets.
460	2. **Fast-backend gate:** choose a backend from conformance and workload data,
461	   not a single raw-syscall microbenchmark. Preserve the synchronous-subset
462	   option rather than forcing false shared-API parity.
463	3. **Schedule-search gate:** never attach an outcome to a requested schedule
464	   that did not execute. Report a critical pair only after a final passing and
465	   failing A/B replay validates that difference.
466	4. **QEMU gate:** establish strict TCG replay with immutable inputs before
467	   adding open-ended fuzzing, more devices, networking, or KVM.
468	5. **Kernel-race gate:** require a stable guest oracle and a known bug before
469	   measuring schedules/hour or attempting discovery claims.
470	6. **KVM gate:** do not treat the protocol skeleton as a backend. Fund the
471	   Sentry bridge only with a dedicated team and explicit ABI/security scope.
472	
473	## Evidence index
474	
475	Primary task-note sources:
476	
477	- Vision and baseline: `goal-hermit-v2`, `impl-test-coverage-audit`,
478	  `research-test-status`, `research-arbitrary-binary-support`.
479	- CI and runner: `impl-enable-selfhosted-ci`, `impl-expand-selfhosted-ci`,
480	  `impl-runner-namespaces`, `impl-merge-latest-prs`.
481	- SaBRe and instrumentation: `research-find-sabre`,
482	  `impl-build-sabre-upstream`, `impl-finish-reverie-sabre`,
483	  `research-sabre-ptrace-parity`, `research-sabre-upstream`,
484	  `impl-sabre-runtime-stabilize`.
485	- KVM and BPF: `research-kvm-backend`, `research-bpf-backend`,
486	  `impl-reverie-parallel-rampup`.
487	- Performance: `research-ptrace-overhead`, `debug-cpu-bound-overhead`.
488	- Schedule/concurrency: `research-schedule-search`,
489	  `impl-revive-schedule-search`, `impl-schedule-search-ci`,
490	  `research-hermit-stress-testing`.
491	- QEMU/kernel: `impl-setup-qemu-vng`, `research-qemu-syscall-surface`,
492	  `impl-qemu-syscall-gaps`, `impl-qemu-under-hermit`,
493	  `research-kernel-race-testing`.
494	
495	Existing detailed documents:
496	
497	- `ai_docs/kvm_backend_design.md`
498	- `ai_docs/sabre_backend_assessment.md`
499	- `ai_docs/qemu_vng_setup.md`
500	
501	This roadmap should be updated when a gate changes state, not only when code is
502	written. In particular, test counts, CI status, preserved stash references,
503	and open-issue state are volatile and must always carry an observation date and
504	exact repository SHA.
505
